common_prompt: Create ONE entirely new 4:5 vertical SanctusArs artwork for the verified Catholic Gospel. The supplied images are visual references for contemporary composition, color relationships, selective surface treatment and the degree of omission only. Never copy their scene, arrangement, persons, faces, gestures, garments or symbols. The whole Gospel episode supplies context, but the short quoted sentence supplies the single visual idea. This image accompanies the short post: it need not retell the whole passage. At first glance one gaze, pause, gesture, distance or spatial relation should connect to the quotation; allow the viewer to infer everything else. All three candidates must simplify; if removing a figure, prop or wall leaves the quoted relation clear, remove it. Choose camera axis and focal alignment for each candidate from the quoted relation, not from a fixed list or quota. Compare the three scenes together: do not offer three near-identical side views that differ only in distance. A frontal or intimate view can carry a decisive word; a wider view can preserve context that makes a relationship legible. An overhead view may suggest an unseen divine gaze when the passage supports it. A reflection in water, a person seen between others or another partly obscured viewpoint is welcome only when it deepens this particular Gospel meaning, never as a novelty effect. B is the most simplified candidate that still communicates the essential relation; retain enough context when further removal would make it cryptic. Compose a singular contemporary sacred artwork from a few large asymmetrical, mostly smooth matte color fields, purposeful overlaps, one legible human anchor where needed, and substantial active space. Keep fine grain or haze only at a small meaningful transition, never as an all-over filter. Cobalt blue, deep plum, muted sage and ivory are a recognizable family, not four colors that must all appear each day. Use only the colors the scene needs; avoid purple dominance, orange warmth and cold monochrome. Cobalt is not a signal of night: in passages without a stated time, daylight and open-air brightness are welcome. Preserve a restrained sense of the sacred through withheld space, selective light and scale. Whenever Jesus, Mary, a saint or an angel is visibly depicted, place at least one subtle area of textured light naturally with that sacred presence. It may be a soft diffused glow behind the head, a gently luminous edge of clothing or a little light in the adjacent air; choose the one placement that supports the quoted relation. Keep it quiet, local and integrated into the mostly smooth matte fields, including when the figure is small or cropped. Do not draw a hard circular halo, gold disc, dramatic beam, neon outline, glitter or an all-over glow. When no sacred figure is shown, do not invent a figure or halo for this rule. Human forms share the same illustrated language as the space: hands and eyes remain coherent wherever visible, never photographic, faceless, distorted or toy-like. This is modern art with a Gospel anchor, not a full Bible-story diagram, vintage oil painting, textured canvas, picture book, stock digital illustration, vector icon or generic abstract poster. No heavy brushstrokes, impasto, paper fibers, grunge, repeated texture, text, logo, signature, border or reserved text area. Generate fresh from scratch; never edit an existing candidate.

A.direction: A / WIDE BUT EDITED DOWN. Show the quoted relation from a wider position, not the full cast or chronology. Let the passage decide whether a high, frontal or lateral vantage best shows the relationship. Keep enough spatial context when removing it would make the quoted idea unclear; a wide image is more than a small person in empty space. Use the scale of figures that makes the relationship immediately legible, with broad quiet color fields doing much of the work. Remove domestic inventory, extra actors and architecture that merely explains the story. This candidate may suggest daylight even when cobalt is present. Do not recreate any reference path, doorway or pose.

B.direction: B / RADICAL MINIMUM. This must be the most dramatically simplified interpretation that still carries the quoted Gospel sentence. Use a close crop or near-abstract arrangement with one legible human anchor: a listening posture, a partial face, a restrained gesture or a small silhouette oriented toward an unseen presence. Keep two or three large quiet color fields and at most one small accent. Omit the room, table, utensils, supporting cast and explanatory props unless one is indispensable to this particular verse. Let the viewer complete the unseen encounter. Do not repeat the reference's Mary, Jesus, hand, dress or blue-plum divide; find a fresh form for today's words. Preserve the Gospel's emotional relation without becoming a generic abstract poster. No conventional portrait, hand reaching at camera or decorative detail.

C.direction: C / DISTINCT VIEWPOINT, EQUALLY SPARE. Find an interpretive vantage that A and B do not already provide. It could look down, directly face the subject, follow a line of sight, see a reflection, or glimpse the subject between people, only if that perspective serves the quoted sentence. Do not settle for another side profile with a different crop or force an unusual angle just to be different. Let one occlusion, scale shift or cropped gesture reveal the quoted relation. Keep the image as edited down as A, with no tableau, period set or illustrative inventory. It must be a distinct interpretation of the quoted idea, not a recolor or crop of A or B. Do not recreate either reference's scene or figures.

occasion_prompt: Create ONE entirely new 4:5 vertical SanctusArs artwork honoring the commemorated saint or sacred figure named in the occasion data. The person being remembered is the unmistakable visual subject. A saint day honors that person, so do not depict a distant figure inside a wide Gospel-event tableau. Use a person-centered medium composition, an identifiable minimal close crop, or a different intimate viewpoint; keep the figure visually substantial even amid large quiet color fields. Choose camera axis and focal alignment to honor the particular person and their verified meaning, not to fill a fixed set of overhead, frontal and wide views. A frontal or close view often gives a feast-day portrait the needed presence; use it when it serves this person. Compare the three artworks and avoid repeating the same lateral profile. An overhead, reflected or partly obscured view is possible only if the saint remains recognizable and the viewpoint adds meaning. For a joint feast, give the commemorated figures balanced presence instead of making one dominant by accident. The verified Gospel quote and scripture_relation may inform one subtle gesture or attitude, but they are secondary to the occasion's verified identity, meaning and sourced symbols. Do not invent a biography scene, quotation, costume detail or attribute that the sources do not support. One verified symbol is enough when it helps identify the person; omit supporting cast and historical scenery unless indispensable. The supplied images are references for contemporary composition, omission, palette and selective surface treatment only. Never copy their people, faces, poses, hands, garments, scene or color-field boundaries. Compose a singular contemporary sacred artwork from a few large asymmetric mostly smooth matte color fields. Cobalt blue, deep plum, restrained sage and ivory are a color family, not a required four-color set; daylight is welcome and purple must not dominate. Keep fine grain or haze only at one meaningful edge. Whenever the saint or sacred figure is visible, give that figure one quiet area of textured light near the head, garment or adjacent air. No hard halo, gold disc, neon outline, beam, glitter or all-over glow. Faces and hands must be coherent and illustrated in the same language as the space, never photographic, erased or distorted. Preserve recognizable human presence while simplifying secondary detail. No vintage oil painting, heavy brushwork, picture-book illustration, stock digital portrait, generic abstract poster, text, logo, signature, border or reserved text area. Generate fresh from scratch; never edit an existing candidate.

A.direction: A / PERSON-CENTERED PORTRAIT. Compose the commemorated saint in a restrained medium or half-figure view, frontal, three-quarter or another angle that gives this person the strongest presence, large enough that face, posture and one meaningful verified attribute or gesture read immediately on a phone. Use broad active space around the person, but never shrink the saint into a tiny figure or make landscape and narrative setting the subject. No group of bystanders or reenacted episode.

B.direction: B / RADICAL MINIMUM AND CLOSE CROP. Reduce the commemorated saint to the smallest recognizable human presence, such as a partial face with clear eyes, a shoulder and one restrained gesture, or a simple silhouette tied to one verified attribute. Use two or three broad quiet fields and one subtle light transition. This is the most simplified option, not a faceless texture study. Do not repeat the reference person or pose.

C.direction: C / DISTINCT INTIMATE VIEWPOINT. Keep the commemorated saint visually central and substantial, but shift the observer to a meaningful axis not already used by A or B. A close frontal encounter, high view, reflection or partially hidden glimpse is possible only when it reveals a different human aspect of this saint. Do not turn this into a wide narrative scene or distant landscape. Differ from A and B in gaze, crop and spatial relation, not merely palette.
